objectives: This systematic review aimed to consolidate observational evidence on the association between spirochaetal infection and neurodegenerative disease. A secondary objective was to identify gaps in the current literature and highlight areas for future research into the pathogenic mechanisms of neurotropic spirochaetes, to inform evidence-based approaches to diagnosis and treatment.
inclusion_criteria: Studies were eligible if they were published, peer-reviewed original articles; human studies in adult populations; reported diagnosis or seropositivity of spirochaetal infection to a clinically acceptable standard; assessed cognitive function, impairment, decline, or diagnoses such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or other dementias using standardized methods; used an observational design (cross-sectional, cohort, or case-control; prospective or retrospective); and were written in English with full-text availability. Clinically acceptable infection diagnosis was defined as validated laboratory methods appropriate to each organism: for T. pallidum, treponemal and non-treponemal tests used according to clinical guidelines; for B. burgdorferi, validated two-tier or modified two-tier serological testing or CSF antibody index; and for Leptospira spp., ELISA, microscopic agglutination test, or PCR-based confirmation. Cognitive impairment had to be assessed with validated tools such as MMSE, MoCA, or Clinical Dementia Rating, or by formal diagnostic criteria such as DSM-5, ICD-11, or NINCDS-ADRDA.
exclusion_criteria: Studies were excluded if they were reviews, letters, commentaries, grey literature, editorials, case reports, conference papers, or surveys; if they used non-standardized or self-reported criteria for infection status or cognitive impairment; or if they were interventional studies, including randomized controlled trials. Studies relying on self-reported infection status, non-validated assays, or unstandardized cognitive measures were excluded. T. denticola studies were excluded because periodontitis was a major confounder, making attribution to the spirochaete itself unreliable. At full-text review, common exclusion reasons were insufficient cognitive testing or assessment (including self-report or non-standardized measures), inadequate control groups, interventional components or other confounders, insufficient diagnostic criteria for infection, and ineligible publication type. When multiple reports appeared to use the same dataset, the most recent or most comprehensive study was retained.

selection_evidence: The main Results/PRISMA text states that 27 studies were included: 13 on T. pallidum, 13 on B. burgdorferi, and 1 on Leptospira spp. Main Table 1 enumerates the 13 syphilis studies as refs 33-45. Main Table 2 enumerates the 13 Lyme studies as refs 46-57 and 59. The leptospirosis results paragraph identifies the single included Leptospira study as ref 58. The main reference list confirms refs 33-59 are all published journal articles, while refs 25-32 are the excluded T. denticola/periodontitis papers mentioned in Results. Supplementary Tables S4, S6, and S8 corroborate the same included author/year set and study counts.
